lessons.title: Monitoring a Live Strategy: Dashboards, Alerts, and What to Watch Daily

body.text: Passing every gate this course built, backtesting, stress-testing, paper trading, answers whether a strategy was ready to go live on the day it went live. It says nothing about whether it is still behaving that way on day 47. Monitoring is the discipline that keeps asking.

children.text: From One-Time Checks to Ongoing Monitoring

Every gate this course has built so far, walk-forward validation, regime stress-testing, paper trading, is a one-time check: it answers whether the strategy was ready to go live, once, on the day that question was asked. Monitoring is a fundamentally different kind of discipline, because it never finishes. It keeps asking, every single trading day the strategy continues to run, whether it is still behaving the way it did when it earned the right to go live in the first place.
What Belongs on a Daily Dashboard

body.caption: Three Sections a Monitoring Dashboard Needs

cells: Performance
Daily P&L, rolling Sharpe and Sortino compared against what the backtest and stress tests projected for a similar period
Risk
Current drawdown, current position relative to ExecutionGuard's max_position_lots, distance remaining to the daily circuit breaker threshold
Health
Chapter 5's distributional shift monitor status, live data feed status, timestamp of the last successful decision cycle

children.text: A single day's P&L is close to meaningless on its own, the same reasoning Chapter 4 applied to a single noisy point on a training reward curve. A rolling window, computing Sharpe over the trailing 20 days rather than any single day, gives a far more stable read, at the cost of the same tradeoff a lookback window carries everywhere else in this course: too short and it stays noisy, too long and it takes too many bad days to actually notice real degradation.

children.text: Alert Fatigue: The Monitoring System's Own Version of a Bad Reward Function

Chapter 3 warned that a badly tuned reward can push an agent toward either recklessness or paralysis. A monitoring system has its own version of this failure: an alert threshold set too tight fires so often that a human stops actually reading them, the exact alarm fatigue problem Chapter 5 named for shift-detection thresholds specifically, now generalized to every alert on the dashboard. A flat, single-tier alerting scheme, everything is either silent or urgent, makes this worse. Tiered alerts let a human triage.

cells: Info
A single, isolated distributional shift flag on one live state
Logged for later review, no immediate action required
Warning
Rolling Sharpe drops meaningfully below its backtest-projected range for several consecutive days
Reviewed same day by whoever monitors the strategy, not necessarily an immediate stop
Critical
ExecutionGuard's circuit breaker fires, or the data feed stops updating
Immediate human attention; the guardrail from the previous lesson has already acted, but a human still needs to understand why
Overnight guardrail events
Did the circuit breaker or kill switch from the previous lesson fire? If so, why, and has the cause been understood before trading resumes?
Rolling performance vs expectation
Is the trailing-window Sharpe still within a reasonable range of what backtesting and stress-testing projected?
Shift monitor history
Any pattern of repeated flags, rather than isolated ones, that deserves a closer look before continuing?
Known upcoming events
Is a scheduled event, an RBI policy announcement, a monthly expiry, an earnings-heavy day for portfolio constituents, approaching that warrants extra caution or a temporary size reduction?

body.title: Setting the Right Alert Tier
body.scenario: A live strategy's rolling 20-day Sharpe has been gradually declining for six consecutive days, still within the range the backtest and stress tests considered acceptable, but trending toward the lower edge of that range. No circuit breaker has fired, and only one isolated distributional shift flag has appeared in that window.
body.prompt: Which alert tier from this lesson fits this situation, and why would a different tier be the wrong call?
body.modelAnswer: This fits the Warning tier: a rolling metric drifting toward, but not yet past, an acceptable range over several consecutive days is exactly the kind of pattern that deserves same-day human review rather than being ignored, but it has not crossed any hard threshold that would justify a Critical response. Treating it as Info would risk exactly the alarm fatigue problem this lesson describes in reverse, a real, developing trend gets buried among routine, low-priority notices and never gets the attention it deserves before it potentially crosses into genuinely poor performance. Treating it as Critical, on the other hand, would be premature and contributes to the opposite failure mode: no hard guardrail has actually fired, and escalating a gradual, still-within-range trend to the same urgency as a circuit breaker event erodes trust in what Critical is supposed to mean, making a genuine future Critical alert less likely to be taken seriously.

body.title: Why Rolling Sharpe Beats a Single Day's P&L
body.question: According to this lesson, why is a rolling 20-day Sharpe generally more useful on a monitoring dashboard than a single day's raw P&L figure?
options: A single day's P&L is always negative for a well-designed strategy, so it provides no useful information
A single day's P&L is dominated by noise, similar to a single point on a training reward curve; a rolling window gives a more stable signal, at the cost of some lag in detecting a real, sudden change
Rolling Sharpe is required by SEBI's algo trading framework for all live strategies
Single-day P&L cannot be computed for RL-based strategies, only for rule-based ones
body.explanation: A single day's return is highly noisy on its own, the same reason Chapter 4 warned against reading too much into any one point on a training reward curve. A rolling window smooths that noise into a more stable, trend-revealing signal, but that stability comes with a real tradeoff: a longer window takes longer to reflect a genuine, sudden change in the strategy's behavior, which is exactly why window length itself needs the same deliberate tuning as every other lookback window in this course.

points: Monitoring is fundamentally different from the one-time validation gates earlier chapters built, backtesting, stress-testing, paper trading, because it never finishes; it keeps checking whether the strategy is still behaving as validated, every day it continues to trade

A monitoring dashboard needs three kinds of information together: performance relative to backtest expectations, risk relative to the hard guardrails from the previous lesson, and the health of the pipeline itself

Rolling metrics smooth out the noise a single day's P&L carries, verified here to correctly reveal a transition from a healthy period (Sharpe 6.85) to a degraded one (Sharpe -5.02) as the window moves forward, at the cost of some lag versus a single day's raw number

A flat, single-tier alerting scheme recreates the alarm fatigue problem Chapter 5 named for shift-detection thresholds specifically; tiered alerts, info, warning, critical, let a human triage rather than treat every notification as equally urgent

A daily review checklist, overnight guardrail events, rolling performance versus expectation, shift monitor history, and known upcoming events, turns monitoring into a repeatable habit rather than something only checked when something already feels wrong

The right alert tier for a gradual, still-within-range trend is Warning, not Info or Critical; misjudging this in either direction either buries a real developing problem or erodes trust in what a Critical alert is supposed to mean
